title: Short-timescale market randomness comes from internal market dynamics

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Short-timescale market randomness comes from internal market dynamics

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Much of the apparent randomness in financial prices, especially on timescales of minutes or seconds, is generated by the internal dynamics of trading entities interacting with one another, not by external news or changes in the value of the asset.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: particularly on short timescales much of the randomness that one sees is purely a consequence of internal dynamics in the market, and has little if anything to do with the nature or value of what is being traded.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 8, “Implications for Everyday Systems”; section “Financial Systems” (from p. 429), p. 431. Scope: price fluctuations in financial markets

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch08-29: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.63

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Prices, order flow, and some external events are directly measurable, and substantial market data exist. Fully public high-resolution coverage is limited, while unobserved information prevents a clean classification of all shocks. Current resources can estimate endogenous shares for selected markets and periods, not settle the broad claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Align high-frequency trade and quote changes with timestamped public news and scheduled information releases, then decompose short-horizon price variance using market-interaction models and exogenous-event controls. A dominant residual attributable to endogenous order-flow feedback would support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Variance decomposition depends on the causal market model.

Comprehensive high-frequency order books are often paid rather than openly downloadable.

Unobserved private information and news confound endogenous attribution.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Second- and minute-scale trades are public for at least one major class of market, and an event-style split between news and no-news windows is a standard analysis. That split can show that a large fraction of short-term variance is not tied to public headlines. It cannot fully separate internal matching dynamics from private information, so the mechanism remains only partly identified.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Decompose short-horizon price variance into intervals with identified external news and intervals without it, at timescales of seconds to minutes. Variance that remains large in no-news windows, and that is shared across unrelated instruments traded on the same venue, would support an internal source; variance that collapses to the news timestamps would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Unobserved information can move prices in windows that contain no headline.

Freely archived tick data are dominated by crypto, while equity tick histories are often licensed.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.75
analysis feasibility: 0.65
discriminating power: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.5
data existence: 0.6
